e-3019.knowledge_point: Applying the Vector Addition and Scalar Multiplication Rules
e-3019.problem: Calculate $\displaystyle{\int_0^2} [  3 \mathbf f(t)+\mathbf g(t) ] \,\textrm{d}t$ given that $\displaystyle{\int_0^2} \mathbf f(t)\,\textrm{d}t=\left\langle 16, \: 2,\: -2\right\rangle$ and $\displaystyle{\int_0^2}\mathbf g(t)\,\textrm{d}t=\left\langle 2,-4,2\right\rangle .$
e-3019.worked_solution:
From the vector addition and scalar multiplication rules, we have

$$
\displaystyle {\int_0^2 } \big[ \, 3 \mathbf f(t)+\mathbf g(t) \, \big] \, \textrm d t =  \displaystyle {3\int_0^2 } \mathbf f(t) \, \textrm d t + \displaystyle {\int_0^2 } \mathbf g(t) \, \textrm d t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}[3f(t)+g(t)]\,\text{d}t & =3{\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{2}g(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =3⟨16,\,2,\,-2⟩+⟨2,\,-4,\,2⟩ \\  & =⟨48,\,6,\,-6⟩+⟨2,\,-4,\,2⟩ \\  & =⟨50,2,-4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

e-8688.worked_solution:
Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t & =-{\int }_{2}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-⟨-3,\,2,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨3,\,-2,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the vector addition rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)+⟨1,\,-1,\,1⟩\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{2}⟨1,\,-1,\,1⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨3,\,-2,\,-1⟩+⟨t,\,-t,\,t⟩{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =⟨3,\,-2,\,-1⟩+⟨2,\,-2,\,2⟩\text{ } \\  & =⟨5,\,-4,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

e-3020.problem:
Calculate 
$\displaystyle\int_{-1}^0\mathbf f(t)\,\textrm{d}t$
given that
$\displaystyle\int_0^1\mathbf f(t)\,\textrm{d}t= \left\langle \dfrac{3}{2}, \: 1, \: 3 \right\rangle$
and
$\displaystyle\int_{-1}^1\mathbf f(t)\,\textrm{d}t=\left\langle 0, \: 2, \: 6 \right\rangle.$
e-3020.worked_solution:
Using the adjacent intervals, we get

$$
\int_{-1}^1\mathbf f(t)\,\textrm{d}t=\int_{-1}^0\mathbf f(t)\,\textrm{d}t+\int_0^1\mathbf f(t)\,\textrm{d}t .
$$

We can rearrange the above as follows:

$$
\int_{-1}^0\mathbf f(t)\,\textrm{d}t = 
\int_{-1}^1\mathbf f(t)\,\textrm{d}t - \int_0^1\mathbf f(t)\,\textrm{d}t
$$

Finally, using the given information, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨0,\,2,\,6⟩-⟨\frac{3}{2},\,1,\,3⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{3}{2},\,1,\,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

e-3021.problem:
Find $\displaystyle {\int_0^1 }  \mathbf c \times \mathbf f(t)  \, \textrm d t$ 
given that 
$\displaystyle\int_0^1\mathbf f(t)\,\textrm d t = \mathbf i-3\,\mathbf j-4\,\mathbf k$ 
and 
$\mathbf c=\mathbf j-\mathbf k .$
e-3021.worked_solution:
The cross-product rule states that

$$
{\int_0^1 } \mathbf c \times \mathbf f(t) \, \textrm d t =  \mathbf c \times {\int_0^1 } \mathbf f(t) \, \textrm d t  .
$$

 

Applying the cross-product rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}c\times f(t)\,\text{d}t & =c\times {\int }_{0}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(j-k)\times (i-3\,j-4\,k) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -3 & -4\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -3 & -4\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}|k \\  & =(-4-3)i-(0+1)j+(0-1)k \\  & =-7\,i-\,j-\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

a
 ⟨−3−ln⁡2,−10,4⟩
b
 ⟨ln⁡2,−5,2⟩
c

 ⟨ln⁡2−1,2,−2⟩

decision.explanation: By linearity, the integral is 3⟨-1,-2,1⟩−⟨ln 2,4,-1⟩=⟨-3−ln 2,-10,4⟩, which is option a.

after.worked_solution:
From the vector addition and scalar multiplication rules, we have

$$
{\int }_{0}^{4}[3f(t)-g(t)]\,\text{d}t=3{\int }_{0}^{4}f(t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{4}g(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{4}[3f(t)-g(t)]\,\text{d}t & =3{\int }_{0}^{4}f(t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{4}g(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =3⟨-1,\,-2,\,1⟩-⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡2,\,4,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,\,-6,\,3⟩-⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡2,\,4,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨-3-\operatorname{ln}⁡2,\,-10,\,4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

after.html:
Question 1
?

Calculate ∫04[3f(t)−g(t)]dt given that ∫04f(t)dt=⟨−1,−2,1⟩ and ∫04g(t)dt=⟨ln⁡2,4,−1⟩.

a
 ⟨−3−ln⁡2,−10,4⟩
b
 ⟨ln⁡2,−5,2⟩
c
 ⟨2−ln⁡2,−8,6⟩
d
 ⟨ln⁡2−1,2,−2⟩
e
 ⟨2+ln⁡2,−6,1⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

From the vector addition and scalar multiplication rules, we have

∫04[3f(t)−g(t)]dt=3∫04f(t)dt−∫04g(t)dt.

Therefore,

∫04[3f(t)−g(t)]dt=3∫04f(t)dt−∫04g(t)dt=3⟨−1,−2,1⟩−⟨ln⁡2,4,−1⟩=⟨−3,−6,3⟩−⟨ln⁡2,4,−1⟩=⟨−3−ln⁡2,−10,4⟩.

content.knowledge_point: Applying the Vector Addition and Scalar Multiplication Rules
content.worked_solution:
From the vector addition and scalar multiplication rules, we have

$$
{\int }_{0}^{4}[3f(t)-g(t)]\,\text{d}t=3{\int }_{0}^{4}f(t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{4}g(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{4}[3f(t)-g(t)]\,\text{d}t & =3{\int }_{0}^{4}f(t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{4}g(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =3⟨-1,\,-2,\,1⟩-⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡2,\,4,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,\,-6,\,3⟩-⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡2,\,4,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨-3-\operatorname{ln}⁡2,\,-10,\,4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Calculate ∫13[f(t)+4g(t)]dt given that ∫13f(t)dt=⟨ln⁡3,3−1,2⟩ and ∫13g(t)dt=⟨34,12,−52⟩.

a
⟨ln⁡3,3,1⟩
b
⟨3+ln⁡3,3+1,−8⟩
c
⟨8+ln⁡3,3+1,−12⟩
d
⟨−8+ln⁡3,1,0⟩
e
⟨3−ln⁡3,3−3,8⟩
Submit

decision.explanation: By linearity, the integral equals ⟨ln 3,√3−1,2⟩+4⟨3/4,1/2,−5/2⟩=⟨3+ln 3,√3+1,−8⟩. Thus option b is correct.

after.name: Question 2
after.worked_solution:
From the vector addition and scalar multiplication rules, we have

$$
{\int }_{1}^{3}[f(t)+4g(t)]\,\text{d}t={\int }_{1}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t+4{\int }_{1}^{3}g(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{3}[f(t)+4g(t)]\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{1}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t+4{\int }_{1}^{3}g(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡3,\,\sqrt{3}-1,\,2⟩+4⟨\frac{3}{4},\,\frac{1}{2},\,-\frac{5}{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡3,\,\sqrt{3}-1,\,2⟩+⟨3,\,2,\,-10⟩ \\  & =⟨3+\operatorname{ln}⁡3,\,\sqrt{3}+1,\,-8⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

after.worked_solution:
From the vector addition and scalar multiplication rules, we have
 

$$
{\int }_{-1}^{1}[f(t)-\frac{3}{2}g(t)]\text{d}t={\int }_{-1}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t-\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}g(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}[f(t)-\frac{3}{2}g(t)]\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t-\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}g(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2},\,6,\,-1⟩-\frac{3}{2}⟨1,\,-2,\,-6⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2},\,6,\,-1⟩-⟨\frac{3}{2}\,-3,\,-9⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,9,\,8⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

From the vector addition and scalar multiplication rules, we have ∫−11[f(t)−32g(t)]dt=∫−11f(t)dt−32∫−11g(t)dt.

Therefore, ∫−11[f(t)−32g(t)]dt=∫−11f(t)dt−32∫−11g(t)dt=⟨12,6,−1⟩−32⟨1,−2,−6⟩=⟨12,6,−1⟩−⟨32−3,−9⟩=⟨−1,9,8⟩.

content.knowledge_point: Applying the Vector Addition and Scalar Multiplication Rules
content.worked_solution:
From the vector addition and scalar multiplication rules, we have
 

$$
{\int }_{-1}^{1}[f(t)-\frac{3}{2}g(t)]\text{d}t={\int }_{-1}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t-\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}g(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}[f(t)-\frac{3}{2}g(t)]\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t-\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}g(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2},\,6,\,-1⟩-\frac{3}{2}⟨1,\,-2,\,-6⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2},\,6,\,-1⟩-⟨\frac{3}{2}\,-3,\,-9⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,9,\,8⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: By linearity, the integral is (1/2)⟨−6,−2,8⟩−⟨4,3,−1⟩=⟨−3,−1,4⟩−⟨4,3,−1⟩=⟨−7,−4,5⟩, which is option a.

after.name: Question 4
after.worked_solution:
From the vector addition and scalar multiplication rules, we have

$$
{\int }_{0}^{3}[\frac{1}{2}f(t)-g(t)]\,\text{d}t=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{3}g(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}[\frac{1}{2}f(t)-g(t)]\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{3}g(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}⟨-6,\,-2,\,8⟩-⟨4,\,3,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,\,-1,\,4⟩-⟨4,\,3,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨-7,\,-4,\,5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Calculate ∫03[12f(t)−g(t)]dt given that ∫03f(t)dt=⟨−6,−2,8⟩ and ∫03g(t)dt=⟨4,3,−1⟩.

a
⟨−7,−4,5⟩
b
⟨−7,2,5⟩
c
⟨1,−1,−3⟩
d
⟨1,−4,3⟩
e
⟨−4,−3,3⟩
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

From the vector addition and scalar multiplication rules, we have

∫03[12f(t)−g(t)]dt=12∫03f(t)dt−∫03g(t)dt.

Therefore,

∫03[12f(t)−g(t)]dt=12∫03f(t)dt−∫03g(t)dt=12⟨−6,−2,8⟩−⟨4,3,−1⟩=⟨−3,−1,4⟩−⟨4,3,−1⟩=⟨−7,−4,5⟩.

verification.explanation: Linearity gives (1/2)⟨−6,−2,8⟩−⟨4,3,−1⟩=⟨−3,−1,4⟩−⟨4,3,−1⟩=⟨−7,−4,5⟩. This confirms option a and the revealed solution; submitted option b has an incorrect second component.

content.knowledge_point: Applying the Vector Addition and Scalar Multiplication Rules
content.worked_solution:
From the vector addition and scalar multiplication rules, we have

$$
{\int }_{0}^{3}[\frac{1}{2}f(t)-g(t)]\,\text{d}t=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{3}g(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}[\frac{1}{2}f(t)-g(t)]\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{3}g(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}⟨-6,\,-2,\,8⟩-⟨4,\,3,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,\,-1,\,4⟩-⟨4,\,3,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨-7,\,-4,\,5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Calculate ∫02[2f(t)+3g(t)]dt given that ∫02f(t)dt=⟨e2−1,sin⁡2,3⟩ and ∫02g(t)dt=⟨3,−1,5⟩.

a
⟨4e2+3,2sin⁡2+9,12⟩
b
⟨7e2,2sin⁡2−3,21⟩
c
⟨2e2−7,sin⁡2+3,9⟩
d
⟨2e2,6sin⁡2,21⟩
e
⟨2e2+7,2sin⁡2−3,21⟩
Submit

decision.explanation: By linearity, the integral equals 2⟨e²−1,sin 2,3⟩+3⟨3,−1,5⟩=⟨2e²−2+9,2sin 2−3,6+15⟩=⟨2e²+7,2sin 2−3,21⟩, which is option e.

after.name: Question 5
after.worked_solution:
From the vector addition and scalar multiplication rules, we have

$$
{\int }_{0}^{2}[2f(t)+3g(t)]\,\text{d}t=2{\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t+3{\int }_{0}^{2}g(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}[2f(t)+3g(t)]\,\text{d}t & =2{\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t+3{\int }_{0}^{2}g(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2⟨{e}^{2}-1,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡2,\,3⟩+3⟨3,\,-1,\,5⟩ \\  & =⟨2{e}^{2}-2,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡2,\,6⟩+⟨9,\,-3,\,15⟩ \\  & =⟨2{e}^{2}+7,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡2-3,\,21⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-⟨-1,\,3,\,-2⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-3,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the vector addition rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{0}f(t)+⟨1,\,-1,\,0⟩\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{1}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{1}^{0}⟨1,\,-1,\,0⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨1,\,-3,\,2⟩+⟨t,\,-t,\,0⟩{|}_{1}^{0} \\  & =⟨1,\,-3,\,2⟩+⟨-1,\,1,\,0⟩\text{ } \\  & =⟨0,\,-2,\,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Reversing the limits gives ∫₀²f(t)dt=⟨4,5,−1⟩. The constant vector contributes 2⟨2,1,3⟩=⟨4,2,6⟩. Adding gives ⟨8,7,5⟩, option c.

after.name: Question 10
after.worked_solution:
Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t & =-{\int }_{2}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-⟨-4,\,-5,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨4,\,5,\,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the vector addition rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)+⟨2,\,1,\,3⟩\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{2}⟨2,\,1,\,3⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨4,\,5,\,-1⟩+{⟨2t,\,t,\,3t⟩|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =⟨4,\,5,\,-1⟩+⟨4,\,2,\,6⟩\text{ } \\  & =⟨8,\,7,\,5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 11

Calculate ∫03f(t)dt given that ∫−33f(t)dt=⟨4,−2,−8⟩ and ∫−30f(t)dt=⟨−3,0,−2⟩.

a
⟨7,−2,−6⟩
b
⟨7,−1,−10⟩
c
⟨1,−1,−6⟩
d
⟨−7,2,−3⟩
e
⟨11,−2,−3⟩
Submit

decision.explanation: By the adjacent intervals rule, ∫₀³f(t)dt=∫₋₃³f(t)dt−∫₋₃⁰f(t)dt=⟨4,−2,−8⟩−⟨−3,0,−2⟩=⟨7,−2,−6⟩, option a.

after.name: Question 11
after.worked_solution:
Using the adjacent intervals rule, we have

$$
{\int }_{-3}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t={\int }_{-3}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

We can rearrange the above as follows:

$$
{\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t={\int }_{-3}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{-3}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

Finally, using the given information, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{-3}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{-3}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨4,\,-2,\,-8⟩-⟨-3,\,0,\,-2⟩ \\  & =⟨7,\,-2,\,-6⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: By the adjacent intervals rule, ∫₃⁴f(t)dt=∫₃⁶f(t)dt−∫₄⁶f(t)dt=⟨8,−6,15⟩−⟨−2,3,4⟩=⟨10,−9,11⟩, option a.

after.name: Question 14
after.worked_solution:
Using the adjacent intervals rule, we have

$$
{\int }_{3}^{6}f(t)\,\text{d}t={\int }_{3}^{4}f(t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{4}^{6}f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

We can rearrange the above as follows:

$$
{\int }_{3}^{4}f(t)\,\text{d}t={\int }_{3}^{6}f(t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{4}^{6}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

Finally, using the given information, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{3}^{4}f(t)\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{3}^{6}f(t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{4}^{6}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨8,\,-6,\,15⟩-⟨-2,\,3,\,4⟩ \\  & =⟨10,\,-9,\,11⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Since c is constant, the integral equals c·∫f(t)dt=e⁻¹e²−1+e=e−1+e=2e−1, option d.

after.name: Question 20
after.worked_solution:
The dot product rule states that

$$
{\int }_{1}^{4}c\cdot f(t)\,\text{d}t=c\cdot {\int }_{1}^{4}f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Applying the dot-product rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{4}c\cdot f(t)\,\text{d}t & =c\cdot {\int }_{1}^{4}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =({e}^{-1}\,i+j+k)\cdot ({e}^{2}\,i-\,j+e\,k) \\  & =e-1+e \\  & =2e-1.\end{aligned}
$$
